title: Shipping sector backs an International Maritime Organization (IMO) climate deal, but not all of the details
summary: Major shipping companies and their associations publicly endorse an IMO climate deal, but their "support" hinges on weakening critical components. Industry players are actively pushing for softer carbon pricing, diluted fuel standards, and favorable emissions accounting, avoiding specific commitments post-postponement. This predictable maneuver risks another toothless IMO agreement, ensuring continued excessive HFO usage and further delaying genuine decarbonization efforts.
content:
New analysis from the global think tank InfluenceMap confirms, with detailed evidence, broad public support across the shipping and fuels sectors for a climate deal at the International Maritime Organization (IMO). However, differing advocacy positions on key components of the framework, including the carbon price, fuel standard, and rules for counting fuel emissions, threaten to weaken the proposed framework as negotiations resume this month, ahead of MEPC 85 (from 30 November) and the resumed adoption session on 4 December.

InfluenceMap identified high-level support for the IMO Net Zero Framework (NZF) from 13 companies and industry associations. Companies and industry associations alike have emphasized the need for a global framework to provide regulatory certainty for the industry’s energy transition, and reaffirmed their support for the IMO as global regulator. The International Chamber of Shipping (ICS), which represents over 80% of the world’s merchant fleet, and the World Shipping Council (WSC), which represents 90% of global liner shipping capacity, in 2025 urged governments to adopt the NZF as a “carefully balanced regulatory package”. European Shipowners (ECSA) has called global regulation essential “to deliver the energy transition of international shipping.” Other companies and associations that have shown support include CMA CGM, COSCO Shipping, Hapag-Lloyd, Moller-Maersk, Mediterranean Shipping Company, FuelsEurope, Ipieca, Renewable Fuels Association, Shell, and SEA-LNG.

However, in the past year, industry’s support for the Net-Zero Framework has become more cautious. Since adoption was postponed in October 2025, the main shipping associations, including the ICS and WSC, have avoided naming the framework, instead asking governments to “consider all options.” They have not proposed specific changes, but this softer messaging leaves room for a weaker deal. A significant risk remains that the IMO will deliver an agreement that undermines the global shipping industry’s ability to decarbonize, with less ambitious proposals creating a landing zone that moves the IMO away from the net-zero trajectory it agreed to in its 2023 GHG Strategy: net-zero emissions by or around 2050, with cuts of at least 20% by 2030 and 70% by 2040.

The NZF has two linked parts, a fuel standard that tightens over time and a carbon price on ships that miss it, both resting on life-cycle rules for counting each fuel’s emissions. InfluenceMap found engagement on these key elements from 4 industry associations: ICS, WSC, Ipieca and SEA-LNG. WSC supported all three elements. ICS broadly supported a carbon price but pushed for a weaker fuel standard ahead of the NZF’s approval in April 2025. Since then, Ipieca and SEA-LNG, representing oil and gas and LNG fuel interests, have advocated against strict GHG life-cycle rules.

Carbon Pricing: ICS and WSC both backed a carbon price, but ICS argued for a low and narrow one. Ahead of the NZF’s approval in April 2025, ICS proposed a carbon price of USD 10–20 per tonne of CO2e, charged only on emissions from burning fuel, not from producing it. WSC backed a carbon price set high enough to make clean fuels competitive, illustrated at USD 74 per tonne in 2030. Both organizations have had limited public positioning on the policy since April 2025.

Fuel Standard: WSC backed an ambitious standard; ICS argued for a weaker one. In 2024-25, ICS backed a fuel standard but proposed a 30% cut in fuel GHG intensity by 2040, less than half the 65% in the approved NZF. WSC supported the IMO’s fuel standard and its GHG intensity targets. Both organizations have had limited public positioning on the policy since April 2025. SEA-LNG opposed proposals that fuels should meet a minimum GHG threshold to count towards the standard.

Accounting Rules: Ipieca and SEA-LNG pushed to lower fossil fuels’ counted emissions; WSC backed stricter accounting. Since April 2025, Ipieca has advocated for replacing the IMO’s cautious default values for fossil fuels with averages and letting certificates stand in for clean power. SEA-LNG argued that LNG’s production emissions are lower than regulators assume. Both would make it easier for LNG-powered ships to comply.

The sharpest divide is between sectors. Shipping associations have broadly backed the framework’s core elements. Meanwhile, oil and gas sector groups have publicly supported the NZF while pushing at the IMO for accounting rules that would make fossil fuels, particularly LNG, count as cleaner. These rules decide how strict the framework is in practice, so loosening them could weaken it without changing the headline targets. The accounting rules are on the agenda when the IMO’s working group meets on 23–27 November.

Notably, InfluenceMap’s research found that support for the NZF often comes at the expense of regional regulations currently in force. ICS, WSC, SEA-LNG, and European Shipowners (ECSA) have leveraged support for a global framework to advocate against the FuelEU Maritime regulation and the EU Emissions Trading System (ETS), calling for the review, harmonization, or withdrawal of these EU-level regulations following the passage of the IMO NZF, despite these rules already being in force and central to meeting EU climate targets.
